notes.name: Distinct from Ahab son of Kolaiah, a false prophet in Babylon denounced by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:21-22) — this is the far more prominent king of Israel married to Jezebel.

name: Jezebel
family_members: Father: Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians
Daughter: Athaliah, later queen of Judah
associated_events: Married Ahab and promoted worship of Baal and Asherah in Israel (1 Kings 16:31)
Had many of the LORD's prophets killed (1 Kings 18:4)
Threatened Elijah's life after his victory on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 19:1-2)
Arranged false charges against Naboth so Ahab could seize his vineyard, resulting in Naboth's death (1 Kings 21)
Thrown from a window to her death at Jehu's orders; her body was eaten by dogs, fulfilling a prophecy against her (2 Kings 9:30-37)
short_description: A Phoenician princess who married King Ahab of Israel, Jezebel aggressively promoted Baal worship, persecuted the LORD's prophets, and engineered Naboth's death to seize his vineyard; she was thrown from a window to her death at Jehu's orders.

notes.name: Her name became a byword for wickedness; Revelation 2:20 uses 'Jezebel' as a symbolic name for a false prophetess in the church at Thyatira, not a claim that this same woman reappeared.

name: Jehoshaphat
associated_events: Removed high places and sent officials to teach the Law throughout Judah (2 Chronicles 17)
Allied by marriage with Ahab and joined him in war against Aram, nearly dying at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22)
Joined Jehoram of Israel and sought Elisha's counsel during a campaign against Moab (2 Kings 3)
Prayed when facing a massive invading coalition and saw God rout the enemy without Judah needing to fight (2 Chronicles 20)
short_description: A generally righteous king of Judah who strengthened the kingdom and taught the Law, Jehoshaphat is best remembered for a prayer of desperate faith before an overwhelming invasion, after which God routed the enemy without Judah needing to fight.

notes.name: Distinct from Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, the royal recorder (secretary of state) under David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:16, 1 Kings 4:3) — this is the king of Judah, Asa's son.

name: Uzziah
associated_events: Reigned 52 years and strengthened Judah militarily and economically (2 Chronicles 26)
Sought the LORD in his early reign and prospered
Grew proud and entered the Temple to burn incense, a priestly duty not his to perform
Struck with leprosy by God for this act and lived in isolation until his death (2 Chronicles 26:16-21)
Isaiah's inaugural vision of the LORD occurred 'in the year King Uzziah died' (Isaiah 6:1)
short_description: A king of Judah who reigned 52 years and greatly strengthened the nation, Uzziah grew proud late in his reign, unlawfully burned incense in the Temple, and was struck with leprosy for the rest of his life as a result.

notes.name: Called both Uzziah and Azariah in Scripture (compare 2 Kings 15:1 and 2 Chronicles 26:1) — the same king, not two figures. Not to be confused with Daniel's companion Azariah (renamed Abednego) or the priest Azariah who confronted him in the Temple (2 Chronicles 26:17-20).

name: Manasseh
associated_events: Rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed and promoted idolatry, even sacrificing his own son in the fire (2 Kings 21:1-9)
Reigned 55 years, the longest of any king of Judah
Taken captive to Babylon in bronze shackles by the Assyrians; humbled himself and prayed, and God restored him to his throne (2 Chronicles 33:10-13)
After his restoration, removed foreign idols and restored worship of the LORD (2 Chronicles 33:15-16)
short_description: The longest-reigning king of Judah, Manasseh led the nation into notorious idolatry and even child sacrifice; after being taken captive to Babylon he repented, and 2 Chronicles records God restoring him to his throne — a repentance 2 Kings never mentions.

notes.good_bad_neutral: 2 Kings 21 records only Manasseh's idolatry and evil, with no repentance, while 2 Chronicles 33:10-13 records his captivity, humbling, and restoration — a genuine tension between the two accounts, both preserved in the text.
notes.name: This is Manasseh the king of Judah, Hezekiah's son — distinct from Manasseh son of Joseph, the earlier tribal patriarch after whom the half-tribe of Manasseh is named.

name: Zedekiah
approximate_period: Traditional early 6th century BC, c. 597-586 BC
roles: Last king of Judah before the Babylonian exile
family_members: Nephew: Jehoiachin, king of Judah, whom he succeeded
Sons: killed at Riblah before his eyes (2 Kings 25:7)
associated_events: Installed as a vassal king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar after Jehoiachin was exiled (2 Kings 24:17)
Repeatedly sought and then ignored the prophet Jeremiah's counsel to submit to Babylon
Rebelled against Babylon, prompting Nebuchadnezzar's final siege of Jerusalem
Captured while fleeing Jerusalem; his sons were killed before his eyes, and he was then blinded and taken to Babylon in bronze shackles (2 Kings 25:1-7)
His reign ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple, at the start of the Babylonian exile
short_description: The last king of Judah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar as a vassal, Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon despite Jeremiah's warnings; Jerusalem fell, his sons were killed before his eyes, and he was blinded and taken captive, ending the kingdom of Judah.

notes.name: Originally named Mattaniah; Nebuchadnezzar renamed him Zedekiah when installing him as king (2 Kings 24:17). Distinct from Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, a false prophet in Ahab's court (1 Kings 22), and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, a false prophet denounced by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:21-23).
notes.violent_death: Zedekiah was captured, blinded, and imprisoned rather than executed; Scripture does not narrate his death, only that he remained a prisoner in Babylon (Jeremiah 52:11).

name: Melchizedek
approximate_period: Traditional 19th century BC, contemporary with Abraham
associated_events: Met Abram returning from rescuing Lot and defeating the invading kings, bringing out bread and wine and blessing him (Genesis 14:18-20)
Received a tithe of everything from Abram
Cited in Psalm 110:4 as a type of an eternal priest-king
Extensively discussed in Hebrews 7 as a foreshadowing of Christ's priesthood, described as 'without father or mother, without genealogy'
short_description: A mysterious king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham and received his tithe, Melchizedek appears with no recorded genealogy or family, and Hebrews 7 presents him as a foreshadowing of Christ's eternal priesthood.

notes.genealogy_recorded: Hebrews 7:3 describes Melchizedek as appearing in the text 'without father or mother, without genealogy' — a theological point about the silence of the Genesis 14 account regarding his origins, not a claim that he had no actual parents.

name: Herod Antipas
family_members: Wife: Herodias, formerly married to his brother
Stepdaughter: Salome (traditional identification, not named in the Gospels)
associated_events: Divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, his brother's wife, which John the Baptist publicly condemned
Had John the Baptist imprisoned and later beheaded at the request of Herodias's daughter (Mark 6:14-29)
Heard reports of Jesus's ministry and wondered if he was John the Baptist raised from the dead
Sent Jesus back to Pilate during his trial after questioning and mocking him (Luke 23:6-12)
Referred to by Jesus as 'that fox' (Luke 13:31-32)
short_description: The Roman tetrarch of Galilee who had John the Baptist beheaded after Herodias's daughter danced for him, Herod Antipas later questioned and mocked Jesus during his trial before sending him back to Pilate.

notes.name: Distinct from his father Herod the Great, who ordered the massacre of the infants in Bethlehem, and from his nephew Herod Agrippa I, who later persecuted the early church — this is the Herod of Jesus's adult ministry and John the Baptist's death.
notes.king: Mark 6:14 calls him 'King Herod' in popular usage, but his actual Roman-granted title was tetrarch, not king.

name: Annas
approximate_period: High priest c. 6-15 AD; influential until c. 33 AD
associated_events: Served as official high priest c. 6-15 AD before being removed by Roman authorities, but retained major influence afterward
Jesus was brought to Annas first after his arrest, before being sent on to Caiaphas (John 18:12-13, 19-24)
Present among the rulers who questioned Peter and John after a healing in Acts 4
short_description: A former high priest and the father-in-law of Caiaphas, Annas retained great influence even after losing the office; Jesus was brought to him first for questioning on the night of his arrest before being sent on to Caiaphas.

notes.name: Distinct from Caiaphas, who was the acting high priest at the time of Jesus's trial (John 18:13). Annas was Caiaphas's father-in-law and a former high priest who no longer held the official office but still wielded significant behind-the-scenes power.

name: Anna
roles: Elderly prophetess who served at the Temple
family_members: Husband: unnamed, married seven years before his death
associated_events: Widowed after seven years of marriage and lived to old age as a widow
Never left the Temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day
Recognized the infant Jesus as the Messiah when his parents brought him to the Temple, giving thanks and speaking of him to all who were looking for Jerusalem's redemption (Luke 2:36-38)
short_description: An elderly prophetess who worshiped continually at the Temple after being widowed young, Anna recognized the infant Jesus as the Messiah when Mary and Joseph brought him to be presented, and spoke of him to all awaiting Jerusalem's redemption.

notes.name: Distinct from Hannah, Samuel's mother, in 1 Samuel — 'Anna' is the Greek form of the same underlying Hebrew name, but these are two entirely different women, centuries apart.

name: Simon Magus
roles: Samaritan sorcerer who professed belief and was rebuked by Peter
associated_events: Practiced sorcery in Samaria and drew a following who called him 'the Great Power of God' (Acts 8:9-11)
Believed and was baptized after Philip preached the gospel in Samaria (Acts 8:12-13)
Offered Peter and John money to buy the power to impart the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands (Acts 8:18-19)
Sharply rebuked by Peter, who told him his heart was not right before God and called him to repent (Acts 8:20-23)
short_description: A Samaritan sorcerer who professed belief under Philip's preaching and was baptized, Simon Magus was sharply rebuked by Peter after trying to buy the power to impart the Holy Spirit — the origin of the term 'simony.'

notes.disciple: He is recorded as believing and being baptized (Acts 8:13), but Peter's rebuke that his heart was 'not right before God' and 'full of bitterness' (Acts 8:21-23) leaves the genuineness of his profession disputed among interpreters.

name: Belshazzar
approximate_period: Traditional 6th century BC (co-regent until Babylon fell in 539 BC)
roles: Last king of Babylon in the biblical narrative
associated_events: Belshazzar's feast using the temple's sacred vessels
The handwriting on the wall ('Mene, Mene, Tekel, Parsin')
Fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians the same night
short_description: At a great feast, Belshazzar saw a mysterious hand write on the wall; Daniel interpreted it as God's judgment on his pride, and that very night Belshazzar was killed and Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians.

notes.family_members: Daniel 5 repeatedly calls Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's 'father,' but historical records identify his actual father as Nabonidus — 'father' here likely means predecessor or royal ancestor, a common usage in the ancient Near East.

name: Balak
approximate_period: Traditional 15th-13th century BC, during Israel's wilderness wanderings
associated_events: Hiring Balaam to curse the encamped Israelites
Balaam's donkey speaking to stop him
Balaam blessing Israel three times instead of cursing them
short_description: The king of Moab who, fearing Israel's approach, hired the prophet Balaam to curse them — but God repeatedly turned Balaam's intended curses into blessings instead.

name: Sennacherib
approximate_period: Traditional late 8th-early 7th century BC (reigned c. 705-681 BC)
associated_events: Besieging Jerusalem and mocking the God of Israel (701 BC)
The angel of the LORD destroying the Assyrian army in a single night
His assassination by his own sons
short_description: The Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel during Hezekiah's reign, until the angel of the LORD struck down his army in a single night; he was later assassinated by his own sons.

name: Hosea
roles: Prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel
Author of the book of Hosea
associated_events: Marrying Gomer as a living parable of Israel's unfaithfulness to God
Naming his children as prophetic signs of judgment
short_description: A prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel, Hosea was commanded by God to marry Gomer, an unfaithful woman, as a living illustration of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's persistent love in response.

notes.married: Scholars debate whether Hosea's marriage was a literal historical event or a symbolic vision, but the text presents God's command and the marriage itself as real (Hosea 1:2-3).

name: Amos
roles: Prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel
Author of the book of Amos
associated_events: Prophesying against Israel's social injustice and empty ritual
Confronting Amaziah the priest at Bethel
Visions of judgment: locusts, fire, a plumb line, a basket of ripe fruit
short_description: A shepherd and farmer from Tekoa in Judah, Amos was called by God to prophesy against the northern kingdom of Israel's social injustice and empty religious ritual, despite having no formal prophetic training.

notes.occupation: Amos describes himself as a shepherd and 'a dresser of sycamore-fig trees' rather than a professional prophet or the son of one (Amos 7:14), emphasizing that his calling came directly from God.

name: Micah
roles: Author of the book of Micah
associated_events: Prophesying the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem
Foretelling Bethlehem as the birthplace of Israel's future ruler
His prophecy later cited in Jeremiah's defense before Judah's officials
short_description: A prophet from Moresheth in Judah and contemporary of Isaiah, Micah pronounced judgment on Israel and Judah for injustice and idolatry, and famously prophesied that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem.

notes.name: This is Micah of Moresheth, author of the book of Micah and a contemporary of Isaiah — distinct from Micaiah son of Imlah, a different prophet who confronted King Ahab (1 Kings 22), and from the Micah of Judges 17 who made an idol shrine.

name: Huldah
roles: Prophetess consulted by King Josiah's officials
family_members: Husband: Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe
associated_events: Confirming the authenticity of the newly found Book of the Law
Pronouncing coming judgment on Judah, tempered by mercy for Josiah personally
short_description: A prophetess in Jerusalem during King Josiah's reign, Huldah was consulted to authenticate the newly discovered Book of the Law and delivered God's message of coming judgment on Judah, tempered by mercy for Josiah himself.

name: Zadok
approximate_period: Traditional 11th-10th century BC (reigns of David and Solomon)
roles: High priest under David and Solomon
associated_events: Remaining loyal to David during Absalom's rebellion
Anointing Solomon king at Gihon
Becoming sole high priest after Abiathar's removal
short_description: A priest who remained loyal to David during Absalom's rebellion, Zadok later anointed Solomon as king and became Israel's sole high priest after his rival Abiathar was removed for backing a different successor.

name: Abiathar
approximate_period: Traditional 11th-10th century BC (reigns of Saul, David, and early Solomon)
roles: Removed from the priesthood by Solomon
associated_events: Escaping Saul's massacre of the priests at Nob
Serving as David's priest throughout his reign and exile
Supporting Adonijah's failed bid for the throne
Being banished from the priesthood by Solomon
short_description: The lone survivor of Saul's massacre of the priests at Nob, Abiathar served as David's loyal priest for decades but was stripped of the priesthood by Solomon after backing Adonijah's failed claim to the throne.

notes.books_mentioned_in: Mark 2:26 refers to 'the days of Abiathar the high priest' regarding an episode that, per 1 Samuel 21, occurred while Abiathar's father Ahimelech held the office — a well-known point of harmonization, possibly using 'Abiathar' for the wider period associated with his prominent priestly family.

name: Jehoiada
roles: Protector and adviser to King Joash of Judah
family_members: Wife: Jehosheba, who hid the infant Joash
associated_events: Hiding the infant Joash in the temple for six years during Athaliah's usurpation
Orchestrating the coup that crowned Joash king and led to Athaliah's execution
Leading the repair of the temple during Joash's reign
short_description: A high priest who secretly protected the infant King Joash from the usurper Athaliah for six years, then led a coup that crowned Joash king at age seven and restored true worship in Judah.

notes.violent_death: 2 Chronicles 24:15-16 records that Jehoiada died of old age at 130 and was honored with burial among the kings for the good he had done.

name: Phoebe
occupation: Deacon/servant of the church at Cenchreae
roles: Deacon (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae
Carried Paul's letter to the Romans
Patron and benefactor of many, including Paul
associated_events: Carrying Paul's letter to the Romans to the church in Rome
Being commended by Paul as a deacon and benefactor
short_description: A deacon of the church at Cenchreae near Corinth, Phoebe was entrusted by Paul to carry his letter to the Romans and is commended as a patron who helped many, including Paul himself.

notes.roles: Paul calls Phoebe a 'diakonos' (deacon/servant) of the church, one of very few New Testament figures given this formal title, and a 'prostatis' (patron/benefactor) — her exact office is debated among scholars, but the text clearly honors her leadership and support.

name: Junia
roles: Described as outstanding among the apostles
associated_events: Being imprisoned alongside Paul at some point
Being named among 'the apostles' in Paul's greetings to Rome
short_description: Named by Paul alongside Andronicus as a fellow prisoner and someone 'outstanding among the apostles,' Junia is one of the few women in the New Testament possibly identified with apostolic standing.

notes.apostle: Romans 16:7 calls Junia and Andronicus 'outstanding among the apostles' (the Greek could also mean 'well known to the apostles'). Some later manuscripts and translations altered her name to the masculine 'Junias,' but the earliest evidence and most modern scholarship affirm Junia as a woman.
notes.married: Andronicus is named alongside Junia and is traditionally assumed to be her husband, but Scripture does not explicitly state their relationship.

name: Rehoboam
roles: King of Judah (first king after the kingdom split)
associated_events: Rejecting the elders' counsel and increasing the people's labor burden
The kingdom splitting into Israel (north) and Judah (south)
Shishak of Egypt's invasion of Judah
short_description: Solomon's son and successor, Rehoboam's harsh response to the people's request for relief from heavy labor caused ten tribes to revolt, splitting the united kingdom into Israel and Judah.

name: Jeroboam
roles: First king of the northern kingdom of Israel
associated_events: Ahijah the prophet tearing his cloak into twelve pieces as a sign Jeroboam would rule ten tribes
Setting up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to keep the people from worshiping in Jerusalem
The death of his son Abijah as a sign of judgment
short_description: A former official under Solomon, Jeroboam became the first king of the ten northern tribes after the kingdom split, but set up golden calf idols at Bethel and Dan, becoming the biblical byword for leading Israel into sin.

notes.name: This is Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel and the one who set up the golden calves — distinct from his later descendant Jeroboam II, a more militarily successful king of Israel.
notes.good_bad_neutral: Jeroboam's idolatry became a recurring biblical refrain — many later kings of Israel are described as walking 'in the sins of Jeroboam.'

name: Ezekiel
roles: Prophet among the exiles in Babylon
family_members: Wife: died during his ministry as a prophetic sign
associated_events: Vision of the valley of dry bones
Vision of God's throne-chariot
Enacted prophecies such as lying on his side and eating a scroll
His wife's death as a sign to the exiles
short_description: A priest taken into Babylonian exile, Ezekiel prophesied through vivid visions and symbolic acts, including the famous vision of a valley of dry bones coming to life as a picture of Israel's restoration.

name: Athaliah
roles: Queen who seized the throne of Judah by force
family_members: Father: Ahab (2 Kings 8:18) or Omri (2 Chronicles 22:2)
associated_events: Murdering the royal family of Judah to seize the throne after her son Ahaziah's death
A six-year reign over Judah
Being overthrown and executed in Jehoiada's coup that crowned the child Joash
short_description: The daughter of Ahab, Athaliah seized the throne of Judah by murdering her own grandchildren, ruling for six years until the priest Jehoiada led a coup that crowned the surviving child Joash and had her executed.

notes.family_members: 2 Kings 8:18 calls Athaliah a daughter of Ahab, while 2 Chronicles 22:2 calls her a daughter of Omri (Ahab's father) — likely using 'daughter' loosely to mean descendant, since Omri founded the dynasty. She is traditionally understood as the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel.
notes.king: Athaliah is never called 'king' in the text but functioned as Judah's sole reigning monarch for six years (2 Kings 11:3), an unusual case in Judah's royal line.

name: Joanna
family_members: Husband: Chuza, manager of Herod's household
associated_events: Supporting Jesus's ministry out of her own means
Being among the women who discovered the empty tomb and reported it to the apostles
short_description: The wife of Chuza, manager of Herod Antipas's household, Joanna used her own resources to support Jesus's ministry and was among the women who found the empty tomb on the first Easter morning.

name: Dionysius the Areopagite
roles: Convert from Paul's sermon at the Areopagus in Athens
associated_events: Paul's sermon at the Areopagus (Mars Hill) about the 'unknown god'
Converting to Christianity along with Damaris and others
short_description: A member of the Areopagus, Athens's ruling council, Dionysius was converted after hearing Paul's sermon about the 'unknown god' on Mars Hill, one of only two named converts from that address.

notes.name: Later Christian tradition attributes influential theological writings ('Pseudo-Dionysius') to this figure, but scholars agree those works were composed centuries later by an unknown author using his name — Scripture records only that he was converted at Paul's sermon.

name: Apollos
roles: Instructed more accurately in the Way by Priscilla and Aquila
Effective apologist for Jesus as Messiah
associated_events: Preaching boldly in the Ephesus synagogue knowing only the baptism of John
Being instructed more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila
Becoming a popular teacher in Corinth, leading to factional rivalry
short_description: A learned, eloquent Jewish preacher from Alexandria, Apollos was instructed more accurately in the faith by Priscilla and Aquila and went on to become an effective teacher, though his popularity in Corinth led to factional rivalry.

name: Titus
roles: Left in Crete to organize the church
Recipient of the epistle of Titus
associated_events: Accompanying Paul on missionary journeys
Serving as Paul's emissary to the troubled Corinthian church
Being left in Crete to appoint elders and organize the church
short_description: A Gentile convert and trusted companion of Paul, Titus served as Paul's emissary to Corinth and was later left on Crete to organize the church there, the recipient of the New Testament letter that bears his name.

name: Philemon
roles: Recipient of Paul's letter to Philemon
associated_events: Receiving Paul's personal letter appealing for him to welcome back his runaway slave Onesimus as a brother in Christ
short_description: A wealthy Christian in Colossae and friend of Paul, Philemon received Paul's personal letter appealing for him to forgive and welcome back his runaway slave Onesimus as a brother in Christ rather than as property.

notes.family_members: Philemon 1:2 greets 'Apphia our sister' and 'Archippus our fellow soldier' alongside Philemon — tradition holds Apphia was his wife and Archippus possibly his son, but Scripture does not state this explicitly.
notes.associated_people: Onesimus (already in this database) was Philemon's slave who fled and later became useful to Paul; the letter is Paul's appeal for Philemon to receive him back without punishment.

name: Gehazi
associated_events: Helping arrange the raising of the Shunammite woman's son
Deceitfully pursuing payment from Naaman after Elisha refused it
Being struck with Naaman's leprosy as judgment for his greed and lying
Later recounting Elisha's miracles to King Jehoram
short_description: The servant of the prophet Elisha, Gehazi secretly lied to extract payment from Naaman after Elisha healed him of leprosy free of charge, and was struck with that very leprosy as a result.

name: Mary of Bethany
roles: Sister of Martha and Lazarus of Bethany
Anointed Jesus's feet with expensive perfume
associated_events: Sitting at Jesus's feet listening to his teaching while Martha served
Lazarus's death and resurrection
Anointing Jesus's feet with costly perfume at Bethany, an act Jesus said would be remembered wherever the gospel is preached
short_description: The sister of Martha and Lazarus in Bethany, Mary is remembered for sitting at Jesus's feet to learn from him and for anointing his feet with costly perfume shortly before his death.

notes.name: Mary of Bethany is a distinct person from Mary Magdalene (already in this database) — the Gospels never identify the two as the same woman, though popular tradition and art have long confused them.
notes.books_mentioned_in: John's Gospel explicitly names Mary of Bethany as the woman who anointed Jesus (John 12:3). Matthew and Mark describe a similar anointing at Bethany but do not name the woman, so this entry lists only the passages that explicitly identify her by name.

name: Salome
roles: One of the women who went to the tomb with spices
family_members: Possibly mother of: James and John, sons of Zebedee (by comparing Matthew 27:56 and Mark 15:40)
associated_people: Mary the mother of James and Joseph
associated_events: Watching the crucifixion from a distance with the other women
Going to Jesus's tomb with spices on the first day of the week and finding it empty
short_description: One of the women who followed Jesus, Salome witnessed his crucifixion from a distance and was among those who came to his tomb with spices on the resurrection morning; comparing parallel Gospel accounts suggests she was the mother of the apostles James and John.

notes.name: This Salome is a named follower of Jesus in Mark 15:40 and 16:1 — she is NOT the unnamed daughter of Herodias who danced for Herod Antipas and requested John the Baptist's head (Mark 6:22-28). That dancer is never called 'Salome' in Scripture itself (the name comes only from the extra-biblical historian Josephus), so she is not treated as a separate biblical character in this database.
notes.family_members: Mark 15:40 names the women at the cross as 'Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome.' Matthew 27:56's parallel list has 'the mother of Zebedee's sons' in Salome's position, leading most scholars to identify Salome as the mother of James and John — a comparison across the two Gospels, not a direct statement in either verse alone.

name: Reuben
roles: Head of the tribe of Reuben
family_members: Brothers: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin
associated_events: Persuading his brothers to spare Joseph's life and throw him in a pit rather than kill him
Sleeping with his father's concubine Bilhah, which cost him his birthright blessing
Offering his own two sons as a pledge to Jacob for Benjamin's safety in Egypt
short_description: Jacob's firstborn son by Leah, Reuben talked his brothers out of killing Joseph but later lost his birthright status after sleeping with his father's concubine Bilhah.

notes.good_bad_neutral: Reuben tried to save Joseph's life (Genesis 37:21-22) but also violated his father's concubine Bilhah (Genesis 35:22), which Jacob cites when denying him the firstborn's blessing (Genesis 49:3-4).

name: Benjamin
roles: Head of the tribe of Benjamin
family_members: Half-brothers: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun
Sons: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, and others
associated_events: Rachel dying in childbirth while naming him Ben-oni ("son of my sorrow"), renamed Benjamin ("son of my right hand") by Jacob
Being held back from the first trip to Egypt out of Jacob's fear of losing him too
Joseph planting a silver cup in his sack to test his brothers
Being singled out by Joseph for a portion five times larger than his brothers' at the reunion feast
short_description: The youngest of Jacob's twelve sons and Joseph's only full brother, Benjamin's mother Rachel died giving birth to him, and he became the focus of Joseph's test of his brothers in Egypt.

notes.name: His mother named him Ben-oni ("son of my sorrow") as she died; Jacob renamed him Benjamin ("son of my right hand"). Genesis 35:18.

name: Tamar
roles: Ancestor of David and Jesus through Perez
associated_events: Being widowed twice after her husbands Er and Onan were struck dead by the LORD
Disguising herself as a prostitute to trick Judah into fathering a child after he withheld his third son from her
Judah publicly declaring "She is more righteous than I" when confronted with proof of the child's father
Giving birth to twins, Perez and Zerah, who struggled over who would be born first
short_description: Widowed twice by Judah's sons, Tamar disguised herself and tricked her father-in-law Judah into fathering her children, becoming an ancestor of David and Jesus.

notes.name: This is Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law from Genesis 38 — not to be confused with King David's daughter Tamar (2 Samuel 13), a different woman roughly nine centuries later.

name: Levi
roles: Ancestor of the priestly tribe of Levi (Moses, Aaron, and all priests descend from him)
family_members: Brothers: Reuben, Simeon, Judah, and others
associated_events: Joining his brother Simeon in avenging their sister Dinah's rape by slaughtering the men of Shechem
Being rebuked and scattered among Israel in Jacob's deathbed prophecy because of his violence
That scattering later being transformed into the honor of the priesthood, since Levites received cities throughout Israel instead of one tribal territory
short_description: Jacob's third son, Levi took bloody revenge on the city of Shechem for his sister Dinah's rape and was cursed with scattering in Jacob's final blessing — a scattering later reshaped into the priestly tribe's dispersed cities.

notes.priest: Levi himself was not a priest; the priesthood was instituted generations later through his descendant Aaron (Exodus 28-29), though the whole tribe of Levi was set apart for sanctuary service.

name: Shamgar
associated_events: Killing 600 Philistines with an ox goad, delivering Israel
short_description: A judge of Israel who single-handedly killed 600 Philistines with an ox goad, delivering Israel in a period of oppression.

notes.genealogy_recorded: Called "son of Anath" (Judges 3:31); Scripture records almost nothing else about him — no other family, deeds, or length of judgeship.

name: Tola
associated_events: Judging Israel for 23 years while living in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim
short_description: A judge from the tribe of Issachar who rose to save Israel and led it for 23 years, living in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.

name: Jair
family_members: 30 sons who rode 30 donkeys and controlled 30 towns called Havvoth-jair
associated_events: Judging Israel for 22 years
Having 30 sons who rode 30 donkeys and controlled 30 towns in Gilead known as Havvoth-jair
short_description: A judge from Gilead who led Israel for 22 years; his 30 sons rode 30 donkeys and ruled 30 towns known as Havvoth-jair.

notes.name: Distinct from Jair the father of Elhanan mentioned in 1 Chronicles 20:5, and from Jair in the book of Esther (Mordecai's ancestor, Esther 2:5) — an unrelated later figure.

name: Ibzan
family_members: 30 daughters, given in marriage outside his clan
30 daughters-in-law brought in for his sons
associated_events: Judging Israel for 7 years from Bethlehem
Arranging marriages for his 30 sons and 30 daughters outside his own clan
short_description: A judge from Bethlehem who led Israel for 7 years and arranged marriages for his 30 sons and 30 daughters.

notes.name: Some scholars locate his Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) rather than Bethlehem of Judah; the text does not specify, so this is debated.

name: Elon
associated_events: Judging Israel for 10 years
Being buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun
short_description: A judge from the tribe of Zebulun who led Israel for 10 years and was buried at Aijalon.

notes.name: Called "Elon the Zebulunite" — Scripture gives no family details or specific deeds for him beyond the length of his judgeship.

name: Abdon
associated_events: Judging Israel for 8 years from Pirathon in the land of Ephraim
Having 40 sons and 30 grandsons who rode 70 donkeys
short_description: The last of the minor judges listed in Judges 10-12, Abdon led Israel for 8 years from Pirathon in Ephraim; his 40 sons and 30 grandsons rode 70 donkeys.

name: Omri
roles: Founder of Samaria as Israel's capital
associated_events: Being proclaimed king by the army after commander Zimri's 7-day usurpation and suicide
Defeating rival claimant Tibni for the throne
Buying the hill of Samaria and building it as Israel's new capital
Being condemned by Scripture as more evil than any king before him
short_description: A military commander who seized Israel's throne after a civil war, Omri founded Samaria as the new capital and established a dynasty, though Scripture calls him more evil than any king before him.

notes.books_mentioned_in: Micah 6:16 condemns Israel for following "the statutes of Omri," showing his influence lasted over a century after his death.

name: Asa
associated_events: Removing his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother for making an idol
Defeating a massive Cushite army under Zerah after praying for the LORD's help
Leading early religious reforms, removing idols and shrine prostitutes
Late in his reign, hiring the king of Aram to attack Israel instead of trusting God, and being afflicted with a disease in his feet
short_description: King of Judah for 41 years, Asa led early reforms tearing down idols and defeated a huge Cushite invasion through prayer, but late in life relied on a foreign alliance instead of God and was afflicted with a disease in his feet.

name: Joash of Judah
roles: Boy king hidden and protected from Athaliah's purge
associated_events: Being hidden in the Temple for 6 years as an infant by his aunt Jehosheba to escape Athaliah's massacre of the royal family
Being crowned king at age 7 in a coup led by the priest Jehoiada
Repairing the Temple of the LORD
Turning to idolatry after Jehoiada's death and having Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned to death in the Temple courtyard
Being assassinated by his own officials
short_description: Hidden as an infant to survive Athaliah's massacre of the royal family, Joash was crowned king of Judah at age 7 under the priest Jehoiada's protection, repaired the Temple, but later turned to idolatry and was assassinated by his own officials.

notes.name: This is Joash king of Judah (2 Kings 11-12), distinct from Jehoash/Joash king of Israel, a later contemporary of the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 13:9-13) in the northern kingdom.

name: Jotham
associated_events: Governing Judah as regent while his father Uzziah was quarantined with leprosy
Building the upper gate of the Temple and fortifying towns in the hill country
Defeating the Ammonites and collecting tribute from them
Being commended as one of the few kings who did right, though the high places of pagan worship were not removed
short_description: King of Judah who ruled well, strengthening Judah's defenses and defeating the Ammonites, though the high places of pagan worship were never removed during his reign.

notes.name: Distinct from the Jotham of Judges 9:5-21 (Gideon's youngest son, who told the fable of the trees choosing a king), a different man centuries earlier.

name: Ahaz
associated_events: Refusing to ask God for a sign when offered one by Isaiah during the Syro-Ephraimite war, prompting Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy
Sacrificing his own son in the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations
Stripping the Temple treasury to pay off the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III for help against Israel and Aram
Building a pagan altar modeled on one he saw in Damascus and installing it in the Temple
short_description: One of Judah's most idolatrous kings, Ahaz sacrificed his own son, stripped the Temple to bribe Assyria for help, and installed a pagan altar in the Temple — yet is remembered for refusing the sign that led to Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy.

name: Amon
associated_events: Following his father Manasseh's earlier idolatry rather than his late-life repentance
Being assassinated by his own servants in a palace conspiracy after just 2 years as king
The conspirators being killed by "the people of the land," who then made his son Josiah king
short_description: King of Judah for only 2 years, Amon reverted to his father Manasseh's early idolatry and was assassinated by his own servants in a palace conspiracy.

notes.name: This is Amon king of Judah, son of Manasseh and father of Josiah — a different figure from the Egyptian deity Amon referenced in Jeremiah 46:25.

name: Jehoahaz
associated_events: Being made king by the people of the land after his father Josiah's death at Megiddo
Reigning only 3 months before Pharaoh Necho of Egypt deposed him
Being taken captive to Egypt, where he died
short_description: The son of Josiah, Jehoahaz reigned as king of Judah for only three months before Pharaoh Necho of Egypt deposed him and took him captive to Egypt, where he died.

notes.name: Also called Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11 and 1 Chronicles 3:15. Distinct from Jehoahaz king of Israel, an earlier northern king and son of Jehu (2 Kings 13:1-9), a different person.

name: Jehoiakim
associated_events: Being installed as king by Pharaoh Necho, who renamed him from Eliakim
Becoming a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, then rebelling against him
Cutting up and burning the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies column by column as it was read to him
Dying as Nebuchadnezzar's forces closed in on Jerusalem
short_description: Installed as a puppet king by Egypt and renamed from Eliakim, Jehoiakim later rebelled against Babylon and infamously burned Jeremiah's prophetic scroll in a fire pot as it was read to him.

notes.violent_death: 2 Kings 24:6 simply says he "slept with his fathers," but Jeremiah 22:18-19 and 36:30 predict a dishonorable, unburied death — the two accounts are not easy to fully reconcile, so this is marked unknown.

name: Jehoiachin
approximate_period: Reigned 598-597 BC; released from Babylonian prison c. 561 BC
roles: Later a captive held in the Babylonian royal court
associated_events: Becoming king at 18 and reigning only 3 months before surrendering Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar
Being taken captive to Babylon with the Temple treasures and Judah's elite in the first major deportation
Spending 37 years imprisoned in Babylon
Being released and given a seat of honor at the Babylonian king's table by Evil-Merodach, Nebuchadnezzar's successor
short_description: Judah's king for only 3 months before Nebuchadnezzar carried him off to Babylon, Jehoiachin spent 37 years in a Babylonian prison before being released and honored at the royal table.

notes.name: Also called Jeconiah and Coniah, especially in Jeremiah. Matthew 1:11-12 lists him in Jesus's genealogy.

name: Jeroboam II
associated_events: Restoring Israel's borders "from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah," as the prophet Jonah had foretold
Presiding over a long period of military success and prosperity
Continuing the golden calf worship established by Jeroboam I and being condemned for it
Being confronted indirectly through Amos's prophecies against Israel's wealthy elite during his reign
short_description: King of Israel during a long stretch of prosperity and military success that fulfilled Jonah's prophecy, Jeroboam II presided over deep social injustice that the prophet Amos condemned.

notes.name: Not to be confused with Jeroboam I, the first king of the northern kingdom who split it from Judah (a separate character in this database). This is his descendant, four generations later.

name: Ish-bosheth
associated_events: Being made king over the northern tribes of Israel by Abner after Saul's death, while David reigned over Judah alone
Losing Abner's loyalty after accusing him of taking Saul's concubine
Being assassinated in his bed by two of his own captains, Rechab and Baanah, who brought his head to David expecting a reward
David having his assassins executed for the murder
short_description: Saul's son and briefly a rival king to David over the northern tribes, Ish-bosheth was assassinated in his own bed by two of his captains, who were then executed by David for the murder.

notes.name: Called Eshbaal ("man of Baal") in 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39; "Ish-bosheth" ("man of shame") likely reflects a later scribal substitution avoiding the pagan name "Baal."

name: Darius the Mede
approximate_period: Traditional c. 539 BC; his precise historical identity is debated among scholars
roles: King who received the kingdom of Babylon after its fall
Ruler in the book of Daniel
family_members: Father: Ahasuerus (per Daniel 9:1 — likely a different Ahasuerus than Esther's husband)
associated_events: Receiving the kingdom of Babylon at about age 62 after its fall (Daniel 5:31)
Setting Daniel as one of three administrators over the kingdom because of his exceptional spirit
Being tricked by jealous officials into signing an irrevocable decree banning prayer to anyone but himself for 30 days
Reluctantly having Daniel thrown into the lions' den, then rejoicing when Daniel survived unharmed
Issuing a decree that all people in his kingdom should fear the God of Daniel
short_description: The ruler who took over Babylon after its fall, Darius the Mede was manipulated into decreeing that no one could pray to anyone but him, and reluctantly had Daniel thrown into the lions' den — then celebrated when Daniel emerged unharmed.

notes.name: Darius the Mede's identity outside the Bible is debated among historians — some equate him with Cyrus the Great, others with a governor named Gubaru or with Cyaxares II. This entry describes him only as the book of Daniel presents him.

name: Ahasuerus
associated_events: Deposing Queen Vashti for refusing to appear before his guests at a lavish banquet
Holding a kingdom-wide search for a new queen and choosing Esther, unaware she was Jewish
Unknowingly approving Haman's decree to annihilate the Jews
Being unable to sleep one night and having the court records read to him, discovering Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty
Granting Esther's request to save her people and executing Haman
short_description: The Persian king who deposed Queen Vashti and later made Esther his queen, Ahasuerus unwittingly approved a plot to destroy the Jews before Esther and Mordecai persuaded him to reverse it.

notes.name: "Ahasuerus" is the Hebrew rendering of the Persian throne name also known in Greek as Xerxes, most likely Xerxes I of the classical historical record.

name: Artaxerxes
approximate_period: Traditional c. 465-424 BC (reign of Artaxerxes I)
roles: Authorized Nehemiah's mission to rebuild Jerusalem's walls
associated_events: Employing Nehemiah as his personal cupbearer and noticing Nehemiah's sadness
Granting Nehemiah leave, letters of safe passage, and timber to rebuild Jerusalem's walls
Earlier issuing a decree authorizing Ezra to lead a group of exiles back to Jerusalem with Temple articles
short_description: The Persian king who authorized both Ezra's return to Jerusalem with Temple articles and, years later, Nehemiah's mission to rebuild Jerusalem's walls.

notes.name: Likely Artaxerxes I of the classical historical record; some scholars debate whether Ezra's and Nehemiah's references to Artaxerxes are to the same reign or two different kings by that name.

name: Shalmaneser
associated_events: Making Hoshea, the last king of Israel, his vassal
Invading Israel when Hoshea stopped paying tribute and conspired with Egypt
Besieging Samaria for three years
The northern kingdom falling and its people being deported, traditionally credited to Shalmaneser though Assyrian records suggest the city's actual capture may have come just after his reign
short_description: The Assyrian king who besieged Samaria for three years after Israel's King Hoshea rebelled, ending in the fall of the northern kingdom and the deportation of its people.

notes.name: 2 Kings 17:3-6 credits Shalmaneser with the siege; Assyrian records suggest the city may have actually fallen just after his death, under his successor Sargon II, though the Bible names only Shalmaneser.

name: Og king of Bashan
roles: Last of the Rephaim (a giant clan)
associated_events: Coming out to fight Israel at Edrei and being defeated along with his entire army
His territory, including 60 fortified cities, being given to the half-tribe of Manasseh
His enormous iron bed, over 13 feet long, being preserved as a curiosity in Rabbah of the Ammonites
Being remembered in Israel's worship as an example of God's power to defeat giant-kings
short_description: The giant king of Bashan, last of the Rephaim, Og was defeated by Israel along with his whole army; his massive iron bed became a famous curiosity, and his land was given to the tribe of Manasseh.

notes.occupation: Deuteronomy 3:11 describes his bed as over 13 feet (9 cubits) long, cited as physical evidence of his gigantic stature.

name: Sihon king of the Amorites
roles: King of the Amorites at Heshbon
associated_events: Refusing Israel safe passage through his land and attacking them at Jahaz
Being defeated, with his territory between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers captured by Israel
His conquered land being given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad
Being repeatedly cited afterward, alongside Og, as proof of God's power on Israel's behalf
short_description: The Amorite king who refused Israel passage and attacked them, only to be defeated; his land between the Arnon and Jabbok became the territory of Reuben and Gad.

name: Eglon
associated_events: Allying with the Ammonites and Amalekites to defeat Israel and occupy Jericho, oppressing Israel for 18 years
Being assassinated by the left-handed judge Ehud, who smuggled in a hidden sword and stabbed him during a private audience, the fat closing over the blade
His death triggering Israel's defeat of the leaderless Moabites, killing 10,000 men
short_description: The obese king of Moab who oppressed Israel for 18 years until the left-handed judge Ehud assassinated him with a concealed sword during a private audience.

notes.good_bad_neutral: Eglon is portrayed as an oppressor of Israel, though Scripture frames his rise to power as God's own discipline of Israel for its idolatry (Judges 3:12).

name: Sisera
roles: Commander of King Jabin of Canaan's army
family_members: Mother: unnamed, referenced watching for his return in the Song of Deborah
associated_events: Commanding 900 iron chariots and oppressing Israel for 20 years under King Jabin
Being routed by Barak's forces at the Kishon River after Deborah's prophecy
Fleeing on foot to the tent of Jael, who gave him milk and let him sleep, then killed him by driving a tent peg through his temple
Being commemorated in the Song of Deborah and Barak (Judges 5)
short_description: The commander of Jabin's Canaanite army, Sisera oppressed Israel with 900 iron chariots until his forces were routed by Barak, and he himself was killed by Jael, who drove a tent peg through his temple while he slept.

name: Benaiah
roles: Commander of David's bodyguard (the Kerethites and Pelethites)
family_members: Son: Ammizabad, who later led his division (1 Chronicles 27:6)
associated_events: Killing two of Moab's best men, a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and a massive Egyptian armed only with a club, taking the Egyptian's own spear to kill him
Commanding David's personal bodyguard, the Kerethites and Pelethites
Remaining loyal to Solomon during Adonijah's attempted coup
Executing Joab and Adonijah's supporter Shimei on Solomon's orders
Replacing Joab as commander-in-chief of Israel's army under Solomon
short_description: One of David's mightiest warriors, famous for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day and a giant Egyptian with the man's own spear, Benaiah commanded David's bodyguard and later became Solomon's commander-in-chief.

notes.name: Distinct from other men named Benaiah in the Old Testament (a fairly common name); this is Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest, one of David's mighty men.

name: Amasa
family_members: Mother: Abigail, David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:17) — a different Abigail than David's wife
associated_events: Commanding Absalom's army during his rebellion against David
Being pardoned and made commander of David's army after Absalom's defeat, replacing Joab
Being sent to rally Judah's forces against Sheba's revolt but taking too long
Being murdered by Joab, who greeted him with a kiss and then stabbed him in the stomach
short_description: David's nephew who commanded Absalom's rebel army, Amasa was later pardoned and made commander of David's forces, but was murdered by his rival cousin Joab, who stabbed him while pretending to greet him with a kiss.

notes.family_members: 1 Chronicles 2:17 names his mother as Abigail, David's sister — a different woman from Abigail, David's wife and the widow of Nabal.

name: Jochebed
roles: Mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
associated_events: Hiding baby Moses for three months to save him from Pharaoh's decree to kill Hebrew baby boys
Setting him afloat in a waterproofed basket on the Nile when she could no longer hide him
Being hired, unknowingly, by Pharaoh's daughter as Moses's own nurse through her daughter Miriam's intervention
Being named as an example of faith alongside Moses's parents in Hebrews 11:23
short_description: The mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, Jochebed defied Pharaoh's decree to kill Hebrew infants by hiding her baby son and then setting him afloat on the Nile in a basket, later becoming his nurse.

notes.family_members: Exodus 6:20 identifies Jochebed as Levi's daughter and Amram's aunt as well as his wife — an endogamous marriage pattern reflecting very early Israelite genealogical customs, unusual under later biblical law (Leviticus 18:12).

name: Orpah
associated_events: Married one of Naomi's sons in Moab
Wept and initially set out with Naomi and Ruth toward Judah after being widowed
Kissed Naomi goodbye and turned back to her own people and gods, unlike Ruth who stayed
short_description: A Moabite woman married to one of Naomi's sons, Orpah wept and initially left Moab with Naomi and Ruth, but ultimately turned back to her own people and gods when Naomi urged her daughters-in-law to return home.

notes.family_members: Ruth 1:4 names Naomi's sons' wives as Orpah and Ruth; Ruth 4:10 identifies Ruth as the widow of Mahlon, which implies Orpah was married to the other son, Chilion, though Scripture never states this directly.

name: Peninnah
associated_events: Provoked and taunted Hannah year after year over her barrenness during the family's yearly worship trips
Bore Elkanah children while Hannah remained childless
short_description: The second wife of Elkanah, Peninnah had children while Hannah did not, and she provoked and taunted Hannah for her barrenness, deepening Hannah's grief before Samuel's birth.

name: Jehosheba
associated_events: Secretly hid the infant Joash and his nurse in a bedroom to save him when Athaliah slaughtered the rest of the royal family
Kept Joash and his nurse hidden in the temple for six years until Jehoiada crowned him king
short_description: A daughter of King Jehoram, Jehosheba secretly rescued her infant nephew Joash from Athaliah's massacre of the royal family, hiding him in the temple for six years until he could be crowned king.

notes.name: Called Jehosheba in 2 Kings 11:2 and Jehoshabeath in 2 Chronicles 22:11, where she is also identified as the wife of the priest Jehoiada.

name: Abishag
roles: Object of a dispute between Adonijah and Solomon
associated_events: Chosen from all Israel as a beautiful young woman to lie beside and care for the aging King David to keep him warm
Requested in marriage by Adonijah after David's death, a request Solomon saw as a bid for the throne and had Adonijah executed over
short_description: A beautiful young woman brought in to keep the aging King David warm and care for him, Abishag became the center of a fatal power struggle when Adonijah's request to marry her after David's death led Solomon to have him executed.

notes.married: 1 Kings 1:4 states David 'did not know her intimately'; Scripture never records her marrying, though Adonijah later requested her as a wife (1 Kings 2:17).
notes.name: Called 'the Shunammite' after her hometown of Shunem; distinct from the unnamed Shunammite woman who hosted the prophet Elisha in 2 Kings 4 and from the Shulammite woman of Song of Songs — Scripture does not identify any of these as the same person.

name: Susanna
approximate_period: Traditional 1st century AD, during Jesus's Galilean ministry
associated_events: Traveled with Jesus and the Twelve and helped support them out of her own means
short_description: Named only once in Scripture, Susanna was one of several women who traveled with Jesus and the Twelve and helped support their ministry out of her own resources.

notes.name: This is the New Testament Susanna of Luke 8:3, not the woman in the apocryphal 'History of Susanna,' which is not part of the Protestant biblical canon and has no scriptural connection to this figure.

name: Eleazar
associated_events: Succeeded Aaron as high priest after Aaron's death on Mount Hor
Assisted Moses in taking the second census of Israel
Helped Joshua divide the land of Canaan among the tribes
short_description: The third son of Aaron, Eleazar became Israel's high priest after his father's death and served alongside Moses and Joshua through the wilderness years and the conquest of Canaan; his son Phinehas succeeded him.

notes.name: Distinct from other biblical Eleazars, including Eleazar son of Abinadab who guarded the ark of the covenant (1 Samuel 7:1) and Eleazar son of Dodo, one of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:9).

name: Ithamar
associated_events: Survived when his brothers Nadab and Abihu were killed for offering unauthorized fire before the LORD
Oversaw the accounting of materials used to build the tabernacle
Given charge over the Gershonite and Merarite Levite divisions
short_description: The youngest son of Aaron, Ithamar served as a priest, oversaw the Levites who cared for the tabernacle, and became ancestor of one of the priestly divisions in Israel.

name: Hilkiah
family_members: Son: Azariah (per the high-priestly genealogy in 1 Chronicles 6:13, usually identified with this Hilkiah)
associated_events: Found the Book of the Law during temple repairs in the 18th year of Josiah's reign
Delivered the book to Shaphan the scribe, sparking Josiah's religious reforms
Was sent by Josiah to consult the prophetess Huldah about the book's warnings
short_description: As high priest during Josiah's reign, Hilkiah discovered a long-lost copy of the Book of the Law while overseeing temple repairs, an event that triggered Josiah's sweeping religious reforms.

notes.name: Distinct from other biblical Hilkiahs, including Hilkiah father of the palace administrator Eliakim (2 Kings 18:18) and Hilkiah father of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1) — a common priestly-era name.

name: Agabus
approximate_period: Traditional mid-1st century AD, c. AD 44-58
associated_events: Predicted a severe famine across the Roman world that occurred under Claudius
Bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt in Caesarea to predict Paul's arrest in Jerusalem
short_description: A Christian prophet who accurately predicted a widespread famine in the Roman Empire and later dramatically foretold Paul's arrest in Jerusalem by binding himself with Paul's belt.

name: Herod Agrippa I
associated_events: Executed James son of Zebedee with the sword
Arrested Peter intending to execute him after Passover, but Peter was freed by an angel
Delivered an oration to the people of Tyre and Sidon and accepted their praise that he spoke with the voice of a god
Struck down and killed shortly after, described as being eaten by worms
short_description: A grandson of Herod the Great, Agrippa I persecuted the early church, executing James son of Zebedee and imprisoning Peter, before dying suddenly after accepting the crowd's praise that he spoke with the voice of a god.

notes.name: Referred to simply as 'Herod' in Acts 12; historically identified as Herod Agrippa I. Distinct from his grandfather Herod the Great, his uncle Herod Antipas, and his son Herod Agrippa II (Acts 25-26), other members of the Herodian dynasty named elsewhere in the Gospels and Acts.
notes.violent_death: His death was not an execution but a sudden and gruesome divine judgment — an angel of the Lord struck him down and he was eaten by worms and died (Acts 12:23) — immediately after he accepted the crowd's worship.

name: Felix
approximate_period: Traditional Roman governor of Judea, c. AD 52-59
roles: Roman governor before whom Paul was tried
associated_events: Kept Paul in custody at Caesarea for two years, hoping for a bribe
Listened to Paul discuss faith, self-control, and coming judgment with his wife Drusilla, and became afraid
Left Paul in prison when he was succeeded by Festus
short_description: The Roman governor of Judea before whom Paul was tried, Felix listened to Paul's message with fear but kept him imprisoned for two years, hoping for a bribe, before leaving him in custody for his successor Festus.

name: Festus
approximate_period: Traditional Roman governor of Judea, c. AD 59-62
roles: Tried Paul and referred his appeal to Caesar
associated_events: Succeeded Felix as governor of Judea
Presided over Paul's trial and heard his defense before King Agrippa II and Bernice
Paul appealed to Caesar during his hearing before Festus
short_description: The Roman governor who succeeded Felix, Festus presided over Paul's trial in Caesarea and, after Paul appealed to Caesar, arranged for him to make his defense before King Agrippa II.

name: Gallio
approximate_period: Traditional Roman proconsul of Achaia, c. AD 51-52
roles: Roman proconsul who dismissed charges against Paul
associated_events: Refused to hear the Corinthian Jews' charges against Paul, ruling it a matter of Jewish law rather than a Roman crime
Drove the accusers from his judgment seat and ignored the beating of Sosthenes in front of the tribunal
short_description: As Roman proconsul of Achaia, Gallio dismissed the charges Corinthian Jews brought against Paul as an internal religious dispute, refusing to rule on the matter and effectively protecting Paul from prosecution.

name: Tiberius Caesar
roles: Roman emperor during John the Baptist's and Jesus's ministry
associated_events: His fifteenth year of reign is used by Luke to date the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry
short_description: The Roman emperor whose fifteenth year of reign Luke uses to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry, Tiberius ruled the empire throughout the years of Jesus's adult ministry.

notes.name: Distinct from Caesar Augustus, the emperor reigning at Jesus's birth (Luke 2:1), and from Claudius, the emperor reigning during the events of Acts 11 and Acts 18.

name: Claudius
roles: Roman emperor who expelled Jews from Rome
associated_events: Expelled all Jews from Rome, which brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth where they met Paul
A severe famine that Agabus had predicted occurred during his reign
short_description: The Roman emperor who ordered all Jews expelled from Rome, an edict that brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth, and during whose reign the famine Agabus predicted came to pass.

notes.name: Distinct from Caesar Augustus, emperor at Jesus's birth (Luke 2:1), and Tiberius Caesar, emperor during John the Baptist's and Jesus's ministry (Luke 3:1) — earlier Roman emperors named in the Gospels.

name: Tiglath-Pileser III
roles: King of Assyria who invaded Israel
associated_events: Received tribute from King Menahem of Israel to shore up his own rule
Invaded Israel and carried the Transjordan tribes into exile
Was hired by King Ahaz of Judah with temple and palace treasure to attack Israel and Aram-Damascus
Captured Damascus and killed Rezin
short_description: A powerful king of Assyria, Tiglath-Pileser III invaded the northern kingdom of Israel, exiled parts of its population, and was later paid by King Ahaz of Judah to attack Israel and Aram-Damascus.

notes.name: Called 'Pul' in 2 Kings 15:19 and 1 Chronicles 5:26, an alternate name for the same king found in some ancient king lists.

name: Ananias of Damascus
approximate_period: Traditional mid-1st century AD, c. AD 34-37
roles: Disciple in Damascus who healed and baptized Paul
associated_events: Received a vision from the Lord instructing him to go to Saul of Tarsus
Laid hands on Saul, restoring his sight, and baptized him
Initially objected out of fear of Saul's reputation for persecuting believers
short_description: A disciple in Damascus, Ananias obeyed a vision from the Lord to visit the newly blinded Saul of Tarsus, laying hands on him to restore his sight and baptizing him despite his fear of Saul's reputation.

notes.name: This is Ananias of Damascus, who healed and baptized Paul (Acts 9). He is a different person from Ananias the husband of Sapphira, who died for lying to the Holy Spirit about money (Acts 5) — Ananias was a common name in this period.

name: Sapphira
approximate_period: Traditional mid-1st century AD, c. AD 33
roles: Member of the early Jerusalem church
associated_events: Conspired with her husband Ananias to sell property and secretly keep back part of the proceeds while claiming to give the full amount to the church
Lied to Peter about the sale price and fell dead at his feet, three hours after her husband's identical death
short_description: Together with her husband Ananias, Sapphira sold property and secretly withheld part of the proceeds while claiming to give the whole amount to the church; when she repeated the lie to Peter, she immediately fell dead.

notes.violent_death: Her death was not an execution or act of human violence but a sudden divine judgment that struck her down immediately after she lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:10).

name: Ananias
approximate_period: Traditional mid-1st century AD, c. AD 33
roles: Member of the early Jerusalem church
associated_events: Sold a piece of property and, with his wife's knowledge, secretly kept back part of the proceeds while claiming to give the full amount to the church
Fell dead immediately after Peter confronted him for lying to the Holy Spirit
short_description: Ananias sold property and, together with his wife Sapphira, secretly kept back part of the proceeds while claiming to give the full amount to the church; when Peter confronted his lie to the Holy Spirit, he immediately fell dead.

notes.name: This is Ananias the husband of Sapphira, who died for lying about money from a land sale (Acts 5). He is a different person from Ananias of Damascus, who healed and baptized Paul (Acts 9) — Ananias was a common name in this period.
notes.violent_death: His death was not an execution or act of human violence but a sudden divine judgment that struck him down immediately after he lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:5).

name: Epaphroditus
associated_events: Sent by the Philippian church to deliver a gift to Paul and to minister to him during his imprisonment
Became so ill from his labor for Christ that he nearly died
Was sent back to Philippi carrying Paul's letter once he recovered, having longed to reassure the church he was well
short_description: Sent by the Philippian church to deliver support to the imprisoned Paul, Epaphroditus fell dangerously ill from his labor for Christ, prompting Paul to send him home with a letter of commendation once he recovered.

notes.name: Distinct from Epaphras, a co-worker of Paul from Colossae (Colossians 1:7, 4:12) — a similar-sounding name belonging to a different person.

name: Tychicus
associated_events: Accompanied Paul on part of his journey carrying the collection to Jerusalem
Carried and delivered Paul's letters to the Ephesians and Colossians
Sent by Paul to Ephesus and later toward Crete
short_description: A trusted companion of Paul from the province of Asia, Tychicus served as the courier who carried and delivered Paul's letters to the churches at Ephesus and Colossae.

name: Trophimus
associated_events: An Ephesian Gentile who accompanied Paul on his journey to Jerusalem
His earlier presence with Paul in the city was wrongly assumed by a mob when they saw Paul in the temple, sparking the riot that led to Paul's arrest
Left behind sick at Miletus
short_description: A Gentile companion of Paul from Ephesus, Trophimus's earlier presence with Paul in Jerusalem was mistakenly assumed by a hostile crowd when they saw Paul in the temple, triggering the riot that led to Paul's arrest.

name: Erastus
associated_events: Sent by Paul with Timothy into Macedonia
Identified in Romans as the city treasurer of Corinth who sends greetings to the church at Rome
Later stayed behind in Corinth
short_description: A city official of Corinth identified in Romans as the city's treasurer, Erastus was a co-worker of Paul who was sent to Macedonia together with Timothy.

notes.roles: Romans 16:23 calls him the city's treasurer (or director of public works); it is debated among scholars whether this is the same Erastus sent to Macedonia in Acts 19:22 and later mentioned in 2 Timothy 4:20.

name: Demas
roles: Former co-worker of Paul who deserted him
associated_events: Named among Paul's fellow workers in his letters to the Colossians and to Philemon
Deserted Paul during his final imprisonment, "having loved this present world," and departed for Thessalonica
short_description: Once listed among Paul's fellow workers, Demas later abandoned Paul during his final imprisonment, "having loved this present world," and left for Thessalonica.

name: Crispus
associated_events: Believed in the Lord along with his entire household after hearing Paul preach in Corinth
Personally baptized by Paul, one of the few converts Paul mentions baptizing himself
short_description: The leader of the synagogue in Corinth, Crispus believed in the Lord along with his household after hearing Paul preach and was one of the few converts Paul personally baptized.

name: Sosthenes
associated_events: Seized and beaten by the crowd in front of Gallio's judgment seat after Gallio dismissed the case against Paul
Possibly the same Sosthenes named as a co-sender with Paul of 1 Corinthians
short_description: The leader of the Corinthian synagogue, Sosthenes was seized and beaten in front of Gallio's judgment seat; he may be the same Sosthenes Paul later calls 'our brother' as co-sender of 1 Corinthians.

notes.disciple: It is debated whether the Sosthenes beaten in Acts 18:17 is the same person as the 'brother Sosthenes' named with Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:1; many scholars think so given the shared name and Corinthian setting, but Scripture does not explicitly confirm it.

name: James son of Alphaeus
associated_events: Named among the Twelve apostles chosen by Jesus
Present with the other apostles at Pentecost
short_description: One of the Twelve apostles, James son of Alphaeus is named in every list of the Twelve, but Scripture records almost nothing else about him individually.

notes.name: Traditionally called 'James the Less' (compare Mark 15:40) to distinguish him from James son of Zebedee, one of the inner three among the Twelve, and from James the brother of Jesus, who led the Jerusalem church. Scripture itself never explicitly confirms which James Mark 15:40 refers to; the identification is traditional.

name: Thaddaeus
associated_events: Named among the Twelve apostles
Asked Jesus at the Last Supper why He would reveal Himself to the disciples and not to the world
short_description: One of the Twelve apostles, called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark and 'Judas son of James' in Luke and Acts, he asked Jesus at the Last Supper why He would show Himself only to the disciples and not to the world.

notes.name: Called Thaddaeus in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18, and 'Judas son of James' in Luke 6:16 and Acts 1:13 — most interpreters identify these as the same apostle. He is distinct from Judas Iscariot, also one of the Twelve, who betrayed Jesus, and from Jude the brother of Jesus, traditional author of the epistle of Jude, who was not one of the Twelve.

name: Jude
roles: Traditional author of the epistle of Jude
family_members: Brother: James (leader of the Jerusalem church)
associated_events: Listed among the brothers of Jesus who, before the resurrection, did not believe in him
Identifies himself as 'a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James' in the opening of the epistle of Jude
Warned against false teachers who had crept into the church
short_description: A younger half-brother of Jesus and brother of James, Jude is traditionally identified as the author of the short New Testament epistle bearing his name, which warns against false teachers.

notes.name: Distinct from the apostle Thaddaeus, also called Judas son of James, who was one of the Twelve during Jesus's earthly ministry; this Jude was Jesus's half-brother and was not one of the Twelve.
notes.wrote_biblical_book: The epistle identifies its author only as "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James" (Jude 1:1); traditional interpretation identifies this James as Jesus's brother who led the Jerusalem church, making Jude another brother of Jesus, though some scholars debate the identification.

name: Matthias
roles: Chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot among the Twelve
associated_events: Had accompanied Jesus and the other disciples from John's baptism through the resurrection
Chosen by the casting of lots over Joseph called Barsabbas to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve
short_description: A follower of Jesus from the beginning of His ministry, Matthias was chosen by casting lots to replace Judas Iscariot and complete the number of the Twelve apostles.

name: Lamech
associated_events: Naming his son Noah, expressing hope for relief from the painful toil of a cursed ground
short_description: Son of Methuselah and father of Noah, Lamech named his son "Noah," expressing hope that he would bring relief from the painful toil of a cursed ground.

notes.name: Distinct from an earlier, more infamous Lamech in Genesis 4:18-24, a descendant of Cain who boasted of violent revenge — that Lamech is not included in this database.
